newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan gov't upbeat about '97 economic outlooks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan gov't upbeat about '97 economic outlooks.

text.p: Taiwan will record robust economic growth in 1997 with stocks on a bull run and exporters benefiting from the weaker local currency, the island's official statistics agency said on Friday.
The agency revised upward its growth estimate for full-year 1997 gross domestic product to 6.58 percent from 6.24 percent in May.
"The domestic economy has walked out of a difficult situation and enters a bright future," said a statement issued by the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
The rosy outlooks were substantiated by strong economic growth and low inflation.

It predicted 1997's per capita gross national product would reach US$13,467 and GDP growth 6.6 percent -- the highest annual growth since 6.8 percent in 1992. The consumer price index was forecast to rise 1.7 percent -- the lowest growth since 1988.
GDP grew 6.34 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, down from the first-quarter's 6.83 percent but far outstripping the agency's previous projection of 5.61 percent.

Agency director Wei Duan told a news conference that the drastic second-quarter GDP rise was due to the smaller-than-expected impact of a farm epidemic that erupted on March 20 and strong stock market performance.
"The hog foot-and-mouth disease has been well under control and we have managed to eliminate the damage to its lowest level," Wei said.

An islandwide outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease has forced Taiwan temporarily to ban all fresh and frozen pork exports -- a US$1.55 billion a year industry -- and to slaughter nearly four million of the island's 14 million hogs.
Officials had estimated the hog disease would reduce Taiwan's GDP growth by between 0.39 and 0.50 percentage point.

A booming stock market, which rose some 13 percent in the second quarter to close in end-June at 9,030.28 points, boosted spending in financial and services sectors and the depreciating Taiwan dollar helped the island's export-oriented high-technology industry, Wei said.
The Taiwan dollar has fallen some four percent in 1997.
"All these factors indicate a fairly stable and healthy economic growth," Wei said.
The stock market is not overheated because unlike the economic bubble that burst seven years ago, this year's stock rise was well-sustained by a "robust and healthy" economy."
"Economists participating in today's meeting all agree there is no such a thing as a bubble economy," Wei said.

Taiwan's benchmark stock index has risen more than 40 percent since the beginning of 1997 and a whopping 100-plus percent since rival Beijing test-fired missiles onto the island's doorstep in March 1996.
Many officials and analysts have raised concerns that Taiwan's market, which on July 31 surpassed the 10,000-point threshold for the first time since 1990, may be overheated.
The stock index crashed some 80 percent after hitting an all-time peak of 12,495.34 in 1990.

Taiwan's economic growth in the mid-1990s was somewhere around six percent a year, but that rate dipped to 5.4 percent in the second half of 1995 amid intense political and military tensions with long-time arch rival communist China.

Helped by a range of government stimulus plans and an easing of frictions with China, GDP growth rose back to above six percent in the second half of 1996, but settled at a disappointing 5.67 percent for all of 1996.
The fourth quarter of 1996 showed a promising 6.76 percent year-on-year rise, prompting officials to announce that a solid recovery was under way.
